explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul writes, "I took Titus along also." (Galatians 2:1) So he went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas on one side and Titus on the other. Titus turns out to matter a lot in the next verse.

Silas is a good guess, friend. He was a traveling partner of Paul's too, because Acts says Paul chose Silas for a later journey (Acts 15:40). But on this Jerusalem trip, Paul names Titus: "I took Titus along also." (Galatians 2:1)

Timothy was a disciple Paul wanted to take along on a later trip (Acts 16:1-3). That's a fine name to land on, since Paul had plenty of partners. But for this trip, Paul says, "I took Titus along also." (Galatians 2:1) I mix up my cookie cutter kids' names sometimes too, and I only have six.

That's it. Paul says, "But I spoke privately to those recognized as leaders." (Galatians 2:2) He sets the gospel before them, then he has a quiet word with the recognized leaders. I'd say it's like pulling the head baker aside to taste the batch before the doors open.

The scribes and Pharisees show up all over the Gospels, so I see why they came to mind. But Paul never mentions them in this passage. He says he spoke privately to "those recognized as leaders." (Galatians 2:2)

Paul doesn't say anything about priests or the temple in these verses. The people he names are "those recognized as leaders." (Galatians 2:2) Jerusalem is a big place, friend, so it's easy to picture the wrong crowd.

explanations.answer: That he was running in vain
explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. Paul says he spoke to them "for fear that I was running or had already run in vain." (Galatians 2:2) He's talking about his work spreading the gospel. I know that feeling about a batch I've been stamping for hours.

explanations.answer: That the crowd would turn on him
explanations.explanation: Paul never mentions a crowd turning on him in these verses. His fear is about his own work: "for fear that I was running or had already run in vain." (Galatians 2:2) Crowds make for a good story, but the text doesn't give us one here.

explanations.answer: That the leaders would arrest him
explanations.explanation: Arrest is a scary thought, friend, but Paul doesn't say it here. He says it was "for fear that I was running or had already run in vain." (Galatians 2:2) The leaders in this scene aren't described as a threat to him at all.

I get why you'd think so, baker. A Greek in Jerusalem with a big question hanging over him sounds like a done deal. But Paul says the opposite: "not even Titus, who was with me, was compelled to be circumcised, even though he was a Greek." (Galatians 2:3)

Right, baker. Paul says, "not even Titus, who was with me, was compelled to be circumcised, even though he was a Greek." (Galatians 2:3) Nobody forced it. Titus walked in as a Greek and walked out the same.

explanations.answer: Spy on their freedom in Christ
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Paul says they came "to spy on our freedom in Christ Jesus." (Galatians 2:4) They didn't come as honest visitors. They came in under false pretenses, and Paul saw right through it.
That would be a nice reason to come, friend. But Paul says they came "to spy on our freedom in Christ Jesus." (Galatians 2:4) Hearing the gospel isn't what he says they were after.

explanations.answer: Bring a gift for the leaders
explanations.explanation: If only they'd shown up with a gift. Nobody said anything about a present, baker. Paul says they came in under false pretenses "to spy on our freedom in Christ Jesus." (Galatians 2:4)

That's the word, baker. Paul says they came in "to spy on our freedom in Christ Jesus, in order to enslave us." (Galatians 2:4) Spying on freedom and then enslaving go together, and Paul names it plainly.

Protect sounds friendly, friend, and these men weren't. Paul says they came in "to spy on our freedom in Christ Jesus, in order to enslave us." (Galatians 2:4) Spying and enslaving is a long way from protecting.
Teach is a gentle word, baker, and the verse isn't gentle. Paul says they came in "to spy on our freedom in Christ Jesus, in order to enslave us." (Galatians 2:4) That's the goal he puts on them.
Yes, baker. Paul says, "We did not give in to them for a moment." (Galatians 2:5) Not even a moment. They held firm the whole way through.
I'm glad you checked, friend, but Paul says it the other way around. He writes, "We did not give in to them for a moment." (Galatians 2:5) So the answer is True: not a single moment of giving in.

That's the one, baker. Paul says they held firm "so that the truth of the gospel would remain with you." (Galatians 2:5) The "you" is the Galatians, the very people reading his letter. He was holding that line for them.

A good name matters, friend, but Paul doesn't say that's why they held firm. He says it was "so that the truth of the gospel would remain with you." (Galatians 2:5) What they were guarding was the gospel itself.

Traveling is all over this passage, baker, so that's an easy one to land on. But the verse is about something else. Paul says they held firm "so that the truth of the gospel would remain with you." (Galatians 2:5)

That's the reason, baker. Paul writes, "whatever they were makes no difference to me; God does not show favoritism." (Galatians 2:6) He respects the leaders, but their fame isn't what settles things. God's own view does.

explanations.answer: He outranked every one of them
explanations.explanation: Paul never says anything about outranking anybody, friend. His reason is "God does not show favoritism." (Galatians 2:6) Rank isn't the point, and bragging isn't Paul's move here.

explanations.answer: He had never met any of them
explanations.explanation: Paul had actually met some of them. Earlier in this letter he says he went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and stayed fifteen days, and he saw James too (Galatians 1:18-19). His reason in this passage is "God does not show favoritism." (Galatians 2:6)

You got it, baker. Paul says, "those leaders added nothing to me." (Galatians 2:6) He laid out his gospel, and they had nothing to add. Think of showing someone your finished batch and hearing, "Looks complete to me."
Paul says the reverse, baker. His words are, "those leaders added nothing to me." (Galatians 2:6) So the answer is True. The leaders had nothing to add to his gospel.

Yes, baker. Paul says they saw "that I had been entrusted to preach the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been to the circumcised." (Galatians 2:7) Two men were given two groups. It's the same gospel for both.
Close, friend, since Titus was a Greek (Galatians 2:3). But Greeks belong with the Gentiles, and the Gentiles are Paul's group in this verse. Peter's group is "the circumcised." (Galatians 2:7)

Egypt is a famous place in the Bible, but it doesn't come up in these verses. The verse says Paul was entrusted with the gospel "to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been to the circumcised." (Galatians 2:7) The answer is hiding in the verse itself.

explanations.answer: The same One at work in Peter
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says, "the One who was at work in Peter's apostleship to the circumcised was also at work in my apostleship to the Gentiles." (Galatians 2:8) Two different callings, and one and the same One at work in both.

The leaders in Jerusalem are the ones recognizing Paul's calling in this passage, friend. They aren't the ones Paul says were at work in it. He says "the One who was at work in Peter's apostleship to the circumcised was also at work in my apostleship to the Gentiles." (Galatians 2:8)

Antioch isn't mentioned anywhere in these verses, baker. Paul points to the One who was at work in Peter: "was also at work in my apostleship to the Gentiles." (Galatians 2:8) That's the source he names.

That's right, baker. Paul says, "recognizing the grace that I had been given, James, Cephas, and John…gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship." (Galatians 2:9) They saw the grace on his life and welcomed him.
Paul says it just the other way, friend. He writes that James, Cephas and John were "recognizing the grace that I had been given." (Galatians 2:9) So the answer is True, and they welcomed him.
Yes, baker. Paul says they "gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship." (Galatians 2:9) It's a handshake, friend, and it says they're on the same team.

explanations.answer: A letter for all the churches
explanations.explanation: A letter would be a nice thing to hand over, friend. But no letter is mentioned in these verses. Paul says they "gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship." (Galatians 2:9)
No council seat shows up in this passage, baker. What they gave was "the right hand of fellowship." (Galatians 2:9) It was a simple gesture, and it said plenty.
That's the request, baker. Paul says, "They only asked us to remember the poor." (Galatians 2:10) Only that one thing. Short and clear, with no extra list.

The Sabbath is a big topic in the Bible, friend, but it isn't what they asked. Paul says, "They only asked us to remember the poor." (Galatians 2:10) That word "only" tells you it was the one request.
A yearly check-in sounds reasonable, baker, but no schedule is mentioned. Paul says, "They only asked us to remember the poor." (Galatians 2:10) There's one request, and it's about the poor.

I see why that might sound right, friend. People often have to be nudged toward a request. But Paul says the poor were "the very thing I was eager to do." (Galatians 2:10) Nobody had to talk him into it.
Right, baker. Paul says remembering the poor was "the very thing I was eager to do." (Galatians 2:10) He didn't need convincing. The request matched what he already wanted to do.
